Chapter 1 · From memory

No notes. Walk her order home.

Before any new work, we go back — from memory alone. Last class followed one work order from the moment it arrived to the moment it was paid. If the class can still walk those eleven stops in order, and still say the gate's question out loud, today has somewhere solid to stand.

Today the order stops being a story — and becomes two real jobs, on her grass and on her doors.

Say her name first

She was named once, in Class 1, and she is never named again. If this is a new group, or the name needs saying out loud to bring her back — here it is. Pick the name the class chose, or type it in.

That's her — the 1972 house. Same house, first day of work.
Say it in class

“Close your notes. Walk her order home — all eleven stops, in order. Then tell me the gate's question, and what we do when the answer isn't clear.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Quick way back in: a job arrives as an order. The office takes it in — intake. Before anyone moves, permission is checked at the gate. Then the job is handed to a crew — dispatch — who do the work in the field and bring back proof: the photos. The office checks that proof — QC, quality control — builds the invoice, and sends the file off — submission. Money comes back — payment — and anything still open gets chased — follow-up. Eleven stops. Today you will watch her grass and her locks travel every one of them.

How to run the recall, step by step

  1. Ask for the stops in order, cold. Take the list as it comes — no correcting yet.
  2. Push on the middle, where lists usually blur: “Proof is back. What happens before anyone is allowed to bill?”
  3. If a stop is missing, don't lecture it back. Ask the question that leads there: “The file is sent. Are we finished — or is there one more stop?”
  4. Close in under five minutes, standing at the gate. That is where the second point begins.

If you've done this work before

You already know the stops are not paperwork for its own sake — each one is a place where a job can quietly die. Proof that never passes QC never becomes an invoice. An invoice never submitted never becomes payment. The recall matters because today's two jobs look simple, and simple jobs are exactly the ones people rush past the stops on. Watch for that today.

The line to remember: “A job isn't done when the work is done. It's done when it has travelled all eleven stops.”

The proof — where this list comes from

An honest label for this drawer: the eleven stops are this programme's own order of work, taught in Class 5 and recalled here exactly as Session 6 asks — order, intake, permission gate, dispatch, field, proof, QC, invoice, submission, payment, follow-up. It is a workflow, not a statistic. If a trainee asks “says who?”, the answer is: this is how the work is run in this programme — and every office they ever sit in will have its own version of the same road.

If this is all new to you

The gate is the stop where the office asks, in plain words: are we allowed to do this work, on this house, today? The order says so, the house is empty, nothing about the job looks wrong — the answer is yes, and work can move. But sometimes the answer is not clear. The house might still be lived in. The order might not match the house in front of the crew. When the answer is unclear, the rule is not “go carefully.” The rule is: stop, hold the job, and escalate — hand the question upward to someone whose job it is to answer it. Nobody at the gate guesses.

How the gate works, step by step

  1. The order arrives and is read — all of it, not just the job title.
  2. The gate question is asked out loud: are we allowed, here, today?
  3. Clear yes — the job moves to dispatch.
  4. Anything unclear — the job holds, and the question goes up. Work waits. That is not a delay; that is the system working.

If you've done this work before

Hold this rule up where the class can see it all session, because today's second job lives or dies by it. The secure job is the gate made physical — locks and boards — but the permission question comes before the crew even leaves. If a trainee treats the gate as a formality in this recall, they will treat it as one at a real door. Correct it here, kindly and completely.

The line to remember: “Permission first. Proof always. And when occupancy is uncertain — HOLD and escalate.”

The proof — where the rule comes from

The gate and its HOLD rule are this programme's standing teaching rules, carried from Class 4 and Class 5 into this recall word for word, because Session 6 opens by asking for them back. They are working rules of the course, taught as rules — not claims about any one company's rulebook. In real work, the order in front of you is always the final word, and this class will say that sentence again before it ends.

Chapter 2 · The first jobs

Her first two jobs.

Today, the house the class protected gets her first two jobs. Not the hard jobs. The first jobs — the ones that show the world whether anyone cares about her at all. One job looks after her face. The other shuts her door.

Grass is the house's face. Secure is the permission slip for every job after it. Hold those two lines — the whole class hangs on them.

Say it in class

“Not the hard jobs. The first jobs. Grass is the house's face. Secure is the permission slip for every job after it.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Think about what a stranger sees first. Not the rooms, not the pipes — the lawn, and the front door. An overgrown lawn tells the whole street the house is empty, and an open door invites the street inside. So the first work is not deep work. It is the work that changes what the house says to the world: the grass cut, so she stops shouting, and the secure, so she is shut, locked, and safe to work in. Everything else in this course — winter, debris, damage, money — happens inside a house that has already had these two jobs done.

How the two jobs divide, step by step

  1. Grass works on the outside picture: the lot, the edges, the look of the place from the street.
  2. Secure works on the doors and openings: locks changed, key held safely, broken entries closed.
  3. Grass will come back again and again, on a diary. Secure is done once, properly, at the start.
  4. Both jobs live or die on the same thing: proof. If it isn't photographed, it isn't proven.

If you've done this work before

You know these are the jobs new people underestimate — “it's just a lawn, it's just a lock.” Say why that instinct is expensive: these are the highest-frequency jobs in the whole industry, and the first ones a client ever judges you on. A crew that cannot prove a lawn will not be trusted with a winterization. First jobs are auditions, every single time.

The line to remember: “First jobs are not small jobs. They are the jobs every other job is judged by.”

The proof — where this framing comes from

The two lines on this slide — grass is the face, secure is the permission slip — are this session's memory anchor in the programme, taught exactly as written there and returned to at the close. The claim underneath them is a teaching summary of how the work is ordered, not a statistic: outside first, door shut first, and the rest of the course builds on both.

Chapter 3 · Grass, part one

Grass is the house's face.

Our house has been empty for a while, and the first thing the world sees is her lawn. Grass does not wait for anyone. It grows in sun and rain whether the house is lived in or not — and an uncut lawn is the loudest sign in the whole street that nobody is home.

Before anyone fixes anything inside, the outside must stop shouting that the house is empty.

Say it in class

“Grass is the house's face. It grows whether anyone lives there or not — and an uncut lawn is the loudest sign on the street that nobody is home.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

A Grass Cut is exactly what it sounds like — and it is four pieces of work, not one. Cut means mowing the lawn down to a neat height. Trim means cutting the grass the mower cannot reach — around trees, along fences, beside the walls. Edge means making a clean, straight line where the lawn meets the paths and the driveway, so the whole lot looks cared for, not just mown. Clear the clippings means gathering up the cut grass and taking it away — not leaving it in piles across the lawn. A job that leaves piles behind is not finished, however neat the mowing was.

How a finished cut reads, step by step

  1. The whole lot is cut to one neat height — no missed strips, no untouched corners.
  2. The places the mower can't reach are trimmed by hand tools — tree bases, fence lines, wall edges.
  3. The borders are edged — straight, clean lines along every path and the driveway.
  4. The clippings are gone. What is left behind is a lawn, not a lawn plus the evidence of the work.

If you've done this work before

The failure you have seen a hundred times is a three-word job billed as four: cut and trimmed, never edged, clippings left in windrows. Teach the class to read a finished lawn the way a QC reviewer reads it — corners first, edges second, piles third. If any of the four words is missing from the work, the job is not done, and saying so early is cheaper than a rejected file later.

The line to remember: “Cut, trim, edge, clear. Four words — and a job missing any one of them is not finished.”

The proof — where the four words come from

The four-part shape of a grass cut — cut plus trim plus edge, clippings cleared — is the required-work shape this programme teaches for the job type, and it is labelled the way the programme labels it: typical — always check the order. One order may ask for more, another may spell the pieces differently. The four words are the class's working vocabulary; the order in front of the crew is the final word.

If this is all new to you

Most damage in an empty house is hidden — a damp wall, a tired pipe. Grass damage is public. Every week the lawn grows, the house announces itself a little louder: to neighbours, to the city, and to anyone looking for a house nobody watches. That is why grass comes first in this course, before anyone fixes anything inside. The outside must stop shouting “empty” — and then, as the next slides show, it must be kept from shouting again.

How an uncut lawn talks, step by step

  1. First the grass passes neat — the house starts to look untended.
  2. Then it passes tidy — weeds stand up, and the lot looks abandoned, not just overdue.
  3. Then the street reads it plainly: nobody is home, nobody is coming.
  4. Everything that vacancy invites — complaints, fines, unwanted visitors — starts with what the lawn said.

If you've done this work before

Put the business sentence under the story one: the lawn is the cheapest signal in the whole system, in both directions. A kept lawn quietly tells a servicer, a city inspector, and the street that this property has someone accountable for it. A wild one tells them the opposite — and it does it for free, every day, until somebody cuts it.

The line to remember: “The lawn is a clock the whole street can read — and it never stops ticking.”

The proof — an honesty label

The step-by-step above is a teaching illustration — the typical way an untended lot reads to a street, not a measured timeline with a source behind it. Real lawns grow at their own speed, in their own season. Teach the pattern as a pattern: the direction is always the same, even when the timing isn't.

Chapter 3 · Grass, part two

First — and again.

There are two kinds of grass cut, and the difference matters. An initial cut is the first cut of an overgrown lawn — tall grass, thick weeds, a lot ignored for weeks or months. A recut is the repeat: the lawn has grown again since the last cut, and it needs cutting again. Initial means first. Recut means again.

And a recut only happens if somebody is watching the calendar. That somebody, and that calendar, are coming up in a moment.

First — or again?

Two jobs land on the desk. For each one, decide what kind of cut it is before you open the answer.

Job A. The order is the first grass order this house has ever had. The crew finds grass past their knees and weeds through the fence line.

Job B. The lot was cut three weeks ago and photographed, neat and striped. The grass has grown back since, and the diary says today is the day.

Say it in class

“Two kinds of cut. Initial means first — the overgrown one, the hard one. Recut means again — and again is a promise somebody has to keep.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Recuts run on a diary. A diary, in this job, is a calendar reminder: this house gets cut again on this date, and again after that, for as long as the order's cycle runs. Grass does not send a warning when it needs cutting — it just grows. So the cycle has to live somewhere outside anybody's memory, on a calendar that is checked whether the week is busy or quiet. The client manager watches that diary, because a missed recut is a lawn shouting “empty” all over again — the whole first job undone by a forgotten date.

How the diary carries a house, step by step

  1. The initial cut is done and proven — the lawn is neat for the first time.
  2. The next cut is set on the diary, on the order's cycle, before anyone leaves the file.
  3. When the date arrives, the recut is dispatched like any other job — permission, field, proof.
  4. Each recut sets the next one. The diary only ends when the order's cycle ends.

If you've done this work before

The diary is where good offices separate from busy ones. Anyone can rescue an overgrown lot once; keeping forty lots quiet on a cycle is a system, not an effort. Teach it plainly: the recut is not a new decision each time. It is a promise made once, at the initial cut, and kept by a calendar — and the person watching that calendar is doing preservation work just as surely as the person holding the mower.

The line to remember: “Initial means first. Recut means again. And again lives on a diary, not in somebody's memory.”

The proof — where the diary comes from

The recut diary is this programme's taught handling for the job type: when a grass file is submitted, the recut diary is set, and the client manager tracks the cycle. Cycle lengths themselves are not taught as a number on this page, on purpose — the length comes from the order, and orders differ. What the class carries away is the habit: no grass file closes without its next date existing somewhere it will be seen.

Chapter 3 · Grass, part three

Proving a cut.

In this job, the work is only real if it is proven. The crew photographs a grass job in three stages — before, the overgrown lot as they found it; during, the work happening; after, the finished lawn, wide enough to see the whole lot and close enough to check the edges.

A striped, neat lawn in the after photo is the signature of a good cut. Those straight mower lines are what “done” looks like.

Say it in class

“Before, during, after. Wide to show the lot, close to show the edges. In this job, the work is only real if it is proven.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Before means the lot as the crew found it: full-lot photos of the overgrown grass, so anyone can see where the job started. During means the crew at work: mower running, trimmer in hand, the job happening. After means the finished lawn: wide photos of the whole lot, so the full result can be seen, and close photos of the neat edges and clean lines, so the detail can be checked. Miss the wide after, and a pretty close-up proves only one patch. Miss the befores, and nobody can tell what the crew actually faced. Each stage answers a different question, and the file needs all three answers.

What a complete grass proof holds, step by step

  1. Before: full-lot photos, the overgrowth plain to see.
  2. During: the crew and the tools in the middle of the work.
  3. After, wide: the whole lot in frame, cut, trimmed, edged, cleared.
  4. After, close: the edges and lines, near enough to judge.

If you've done this work before

This is the slide to slow down on, because the verdict exercise at the end of the class is won or lost right here. The classic gap is not laziness — it is a crew photographing what looks good instead of what proves the job. Wide-and-close is a discipline: the wide shot is for the lot, the close shot is for the detail, and neither can do the other's work. Say that sentence twice today.

The line to remember: “Wide proves the lot. Close proves the detail. Neither one can do the other's job.”

The proof — the required shape, honestly labelled

The required proof for a grass job, as this programme teaches it — typical, and always check the order: before photos of the full lot; cut plus trim plus edge; after photos wide plus close; date-stamps where the order's rulebook requires them. The full photo sets for this work type live with the class's photo materials — the worked examples in this session are described in words and stay as words, so the class learns to name a missing shot, not to recognise one picture.

If this is all new to you

A date-stamp is a date printed on the photo itself, proving when it was taken. Some rulebooks require date-stamps on every photo. Some do not ask for them at all. There is no house rule that covers every order, and that is the point: the rule is always the same — check the order. Never stamp because you feel like it, and never skip one because you forgot. Read the order, and do what it says.

How the stamp question gets answered, step by step

  1. Before the visit, the order is read for its photo rules — stamps named, or not named.
  2. If the order requires stamps, the crew's camera is set before the first photo, not fixed up afterwards.
  3. If the order does not require them, the photos go in clean, as taken.
  4. At QC, the photos are checked against what that order asked for — not against a habit.

If you've done this work before

This small rule carries the biggest habit in the course: requirements live in the order, not in memory, not in “how the last client liked it.” A trainee who learns to ask “what does this order say?” about a date-stamp will ask it about lock codes, boards, and prices too. Protect the habit here, on the small thing, and it will be there for the large ones.

The line to remember: “Never stamp because you feel like it. Never skip one because you forgot. Read the order.”

The proof — why this page gives no single answer

This session deliberately teaches no universal date-stamp rule, because the programme's own rule is that the requirement follows the order and its rulebook — and rulebooks differ. Any page that told the class “always stamp” or “never stamp” would be teaching them to be wrong on half their orders. What is proven here is the discipline, and the discipline is: check the order, every time.

Chapter 3 · Grass, part four

One lawn, four kinds of people.

A grass job looks like one person with a mower. It is actually four kinds of people, each holding a different part of the work — and the lawn only becomes a finished, paid job if every one of them does their part.

And one line runs through this slide that the class must never cross. It is in the notes — the owner marks it himself. Always.

OrderThe job arrives and is read.
→
PermissionThe gate question is answered.
→
DispatchA crew is sent.
→
FieldThe cut, photographed before, during, after.
→
Proof + QCThe processor tags and checks.
→
SubmitThe client manager sends the file.
→
Diary setThe recut date goes on the calendar.
Say it in class

“The crew cuts. The vendor manager dispatches and confirms. The processor proves and invoices. The client manager submits and tracks the cycle. Four kinds of people, one lawn.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

The crew cuts — the people at the house with the mower and the trimmer, taking the before, during, and after photos as they go. The vendor manager dispatches and confirms — the person who reads the order, checks the gate, picks the crew, and makes sure the visit actually happened. The processor proves and invoices — the person who turns photos and reports into a clean, honest bill. The client manager submits and tracks the cycle — the person who carries the finished file to the client's system, watches what comes back, and keeps the recut diary. Four kinds of people, one lawn — and every one of them has to do their part, or the lawn stays a lie.

How the job passes from hand to hand

  1. Order → permission → dispatch: the vendor manager's ground.
  2. Field: the crew cuts and photographs, all three stages.
  3. Proof: the processor tags the photos, checks them, and builds the invoice from what was approved and proven.
  4. Submission: the client manager sends the file — and sets the recut diary before the file closes.

If you've done this work before

Notice what each role is really holding. The crew holds the truth of the lot. The vendor manager holds the promise that someone went. The processor holds the honesty of the bill. The client manager holds the future — the payment, and the next cut's date. When a trainee later sits in any one of these seats, they should be able to say which of those things is in their hands. That is what this slide is for.

The line to remember: “Four kinds of people, one lawn — and every one of them has to do their part, or the lawn stays a lie.”

The proof — where the four roles come from

The four roles and their parts in a grass job are this programme's taught handling, told as people rather than boxes, exactly as the session prescribes. Real offices divide the work in their own ways — one person may hold two of these parts. What does not change, in any office, is that all four parts exist, and each one has a name in this class so a missing part can be spotted and named.

If this is all new to you

Ready For Office is a mark that says a file is finished and ready to go. Here is the guard, and the class must hear it early because it matters in every session after this one: the processor prepares the file up to ready — every photo tagged, every check done, the invoice built — but the processor never marks it Ready For Office. The owner marks it himself. Always. The processor prepares. The owner marks. That line is never crossed. The processor records the work in the office engine, called PPW — our own system, never a client portal — and builds the invoice from what was approved and proven.

Where the line sits, step by step

  1. The processor tags, checks, and invoices — the file is complete in every way the processor controls.
  2. The file waits at ready. Nothing about it is unfinished — except the mark.
  3. The owner reviews and marks it Ready For Office himself.
  4. Only then does the file travel onward. No exceptions, no “just this once.”

If you've done this work before

Do not let this sound like a small office custom. It is a control: the person who prepares a file is never the person who declares it finished, and that separation is what lets an owner trust a file he did not build. If a trainee asks why they cannot just mark it and save time, the answer is the whole point of the guard — the mark is a signature, and you do not sign another person's name, however good the file is.

The line to remember: “The processor prepares. The owner marks. That line is never crossed.”

The proof — the guard, stated plainly

This guard is a standing rule of the programme's own office, taught here because Session 6 is where it is first stated to the class — and it is stated as a rule of this office's work, not as a claim about how every company runs. PPW is named for the same reason: it is the office's own engine for recording work, and the class must never confuse it with a client's portal. Two different systems, two different kinds of care.

Chapter 4 · Secure, part one

Secure is the permission slip.

Before grass, or beside grass, or behind it, there is a job that comes before every other job. An open house is not a house waiting for work. An open house is an invitation — anyone can walk in, anything can be taken, and nothing inside is safe.

Secure first. Nothing happens in an open house.

Say it in class

“An open house is not a house waiting for work. An open house is an invitation. Secure first — nothing happens in an open house.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Remember school trips. A permission slip is the paper that says you are allowed to go. No slip, no trip — it did not matter that the bus was there and your friends were on it. This job works the same way. A secure house is the permission slip for every job after it. No secure, no winterization crew walking in. No secure, no debris crew carrying things out. No secure, nothing. The house must be shut, locked, and proven shut before the rest of her story can happen — and a crew should never be working in a place where anyone can wander through the door.

How the slip works, step by step

  1. The house stands open — a risk to the house, to anything inside it, and to any crew sent in.
  2. The secure job shuts her: locks changed, key held in a lockbox, broken entries boarded.
  3. The proof shows her shut — every lock, every board, photographed.
  4. Only now do the later jobs have somewhere safe to happen.

If you've done this work before

You have stood at the door this slide is about — the one that should have been secured and wasn't, with the copper already gone. The teaching point is the order of operations, and it is not negotiable in the field either: a house that is not yet secure is not yet a workplace. Sending a crew into an open house doesn't save a day. It risks the crew, the tools, and whatever is left of the house.

The line to remember: “No slip, no trip. No secure, no job. The house must be proven shut before her story can go on.”

The proof — where the picture comes from

The permission-slip picture is this session's own teaching image, carried word for word from the programme because it does real work: it gives a brand-new trainee a rule they already understand from childhood, and hangs the whole secure job on it. The claim under the picture — that work should not proceed in an unsecured house — is the programme's standing rule for the job type, taught as a rule.

Chapter 4 · Secure, part two

Three parts. Done slowly.

An Initial Secure has three parts. Change every exterior lock, so no old key in the world still opens this house. Set the lockbox code exactly as the order states. And board every broken or weak entry, firm enough that no one can walk through it.

Exactly is the hardest word in this job. Not nearly. Not the code from last time. Exactly.

Say it in class

“Every exterior lock. The code exactly as the order states. Every broken entry boarded. Three parts — and a secure missing any one of them is not a secure.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

First, change every exterior lock. Exterior means outside — every door that leads in from outside gets a new lock: front, back, side, the door from the garage, all of them. Changing a lock so old keys no longer work is called rekeying. The reason for “every” is simple: nobody knows how many copies of the old keys exist, or whose pockets they are in. Change four doors out of five, and the fifth door is still open to every old key ever cut for it. The job is not “mostly rekeyed.” The job is: no old key in the world still opens this house.

How “every” gets checked, step by step

  1. Walk the house and count the exterior doors before touching a lock — all of them, including the easy-to-forget ones.
  2. Change each lock, one by one, and test each new key as you go.
  3. Count again at the end: doors found, locks changed. The two numbers must match.
  4. Any door that cannot be secured is not quietly left — it is reported, the same day.

If you've done this work before

The missed door is the classic secure failure — usually the side door or the garage entry, the one nobody uses. Teach the count, out loud, as a habit: doors found, locks changed, numbers matched. A crew that counts cannot quietly miss one, and a processor who asks for the count catches the miss while it is still cheap to fix.

The line to remember: “Change four doors out of five, and you have changed nothing that matters. Every means every.”

The proof — the required shape, honestly labelled

“Every exterior lock changed” is the first line of the required shape this programme teaches for an Initial Secure — typical, and always check the order. The order names the doors and the details for its house; the class's word “every” is how they make sure none of the order's doors is quietly skipped.

If this is all new to you

A lockbox is a small locked box that holds a key, opened with a code. It is how the next crew — and every crew after — gets into a house with no family to let them in. The code must be set exactly as the order states. Not nearly. Not the code from the last house, not the code the crew usually uses. Exactly the code on this order. A wrong code is not a small mistake: it is the next crew standing at a shut door they cannot open, and a job that never starts.

How the code gets set right, step by step

  1. Read the code from this order — this house, this order, no other.
  2. Set the lockbox to that code, digit by digit.
  3. Test it: close the box, scramble it, open it again with the code, before leaving the door.
  4. Photograph the lockbox in place, as the order asks, so the proof shows it was there and set.

If you've done this work before

Every experienced person in this work has a lockbox story — the frozen morning, the wrong code, the job that died at the door. Tell the class the shape of the lesson without dressing it up: codes are copied, never remembered. The moment a code comes from memory instead of from the order in hand, it is a guess wearing a uniform. And guesses at a locked door are paid for in whole lost days.

The line to remember: “Codes are copied, never remembered. Exactly as the order states — not nearly, not last time's.”

The proof — why this page prints no code

There is no example lockbox code anywhere on this page, and that is deliberate. Codes belong to real orders and real houses, and a teaching page that printed one would teach exactly the wrong habit — reaching for a familiar number. The programme teaches the rule without the digits: the code comes from the order, is set exactly, and is tested before the crew leaves the door.

If this is all new to you

To board means covering a broken or weak door or window with strong boards, fixed firmly, so no one can walk through it. Locks only guard the doors that still work. The broken back window, the cracked door that no longer latches — those are entries too, and an entry does not stop being an entry because it is broken. Until it is boarded, it is an open door with glass on the floor. Every broken or weak entry gets boarded, and boarded firm — a board that gives way to one hard push is a decoration, not a secure.

How a boarding gets done, step by step

  1. Walk the house and find every broken or weak entry — windows, doors, any opening a person could use.
  2. Cover each one fully with strong boards, fixed firmly to the structure.
  3. Test each board the way a stranger would: push, pull, look for the gap.
  4. Photograph every board — a board with no photo might as well not exist, as the next slide will show.

If you've done this work before

The weak entry is the one that teaches judgement: not broken, not sound — the window that latches badly, the door that flexes. Teach the class to board on doubt and report what they found, rather than talk themselves out of it at the door. A board nobody needed costs little. An entry nobody boarded can cost the house.

The line to remember: “A broken window that is not boarded is an open door with glass on the floor.”

The proof — the required shape, honestly labelled

“Each broken entry boarded” completes the required shape this programme teaches for an Initial Secure — every exterior lock changed, lockbox code exact, each broken entry boarded, a photo of every lock and every board — labelled, as always on this page: typical, and always check the order. The order for a real house names its own entries and its own details.

Chapter 4 · Secure, part three

The strictest proof in the course.

The proof of a secure job is the strictest in the whole course. Every lock gets a photo. Every board gets a photo. Before, during, and after, labelled — the old lock and the broken entry, the work happening, the new lock and the firm board.

If one lock has no after photo, the secure is not proven. In this job, an unphotographed lock is an unlocked door.

Say it in class

“Every lock. Every board. Before, during, after, labelled. An unphotographed lock is an unlocked door.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Grass proof can be wide — one good photo can show a whole lot. Secure proof cannot. A secure is a list of single things — this lock, that board — and each single thing needs its own proof. Before shows the old lock and the broken entry. During shows the rekeying and the boarding happening. After shows the new lock and the firm board. If one lock has no after photo, the secure is not proven. If one board has no photo, the board might as well not exist. That sounds harsh until you see it from the desk: the photo is the only way anyone who was not there can know the door is shut.

What a complete secure proof holds, step by step

  1. Before: the old locks and every broken entry, as found.
  2. During: the rekeying and the boarding, in the middle of the work.
  3. After: every new lock, and every board, one by one.
  4. Labels on all of it — because forty unlabeled photos of doors prove nothing in order.

If you've done this work before

Hold the count from the last slide up against this one: doors found, locks changed, photos taken — three numbers, and at QC they must tell the same story. The processor's job on a secure is not “look through the photos.” It is reconciliation, item by item, against the order's list. Teach that word here if the class is ready for it: a secure file is reconciled, not glanced at.

The line to remember: “A secure is a list, not a picture. Every item on the list needs its own proof.”

The proof — the required shape, honestly labelled

The secure proof as this programme teaches it — typical, and always check the order: every lock plus every board photographed, before, during, and after, labelled. As with grass, the worked examples in this session are described in words and stay as words; the class learns to check a file against a list, not to recognise one set of pictures.

If this is all new to you

A secure travels the stops in a stricter order than a grass job: order → PERMISSION FIRST → dispatch → rekey plus board plus photograph → tag plus QC → submit. The crew secures. The vendor manager owns the gate — the person who answers the permission question before anyone moves, and that ownership is the whole job: if the answer is unclear, the job holds, however ready the crew is. The processor proves every lock and board. The client manager submits. Same four people as the lawn — but on this job, the gate is not a stop on the way. It is the front door of the whole job, and it opens first or not at all.

How a secure is handled, step by step

  1. Order arrives; the gate question is asked and answered — clearly, or not at all.
  2. Dispatch: the crew goes out knowing every door and entry the order names.
  3. Field: rekey, set the lockbox, board — photographing every item, every stage.
  4. Proof: the processor reconciles the photos against the list, then the file is submitted.

If you've done this work before

Say the quiet part out loud for the experienced hands in the room: on a secure, a permission mistake is not an office error, it is a person changing locks on a house they may have had no right to touch. That is why the gate sits in capital letters in this handling and nowhere else in the course. The class should leave able to feel the difference between the two handlings, not just recite them.

The line to remember: “On a grass job, the gate is a stop. On a secure, the gate is the front door — it opens first, or not at all.”

The proof — the two handlings, side by side

GrassOrder → permission → dispatch → cut + photograph → tag + QC → submit → diary set.
SecureOrder → PERMISSION FIRST → dispatch → rekey + board + photograph → tag + QC → submit.

Both handlings are this programme's taught shapes for the two job types, carried from the session exactly. The difference between them is the lesson: same road, different weight on the gate.

Chapter 5 · The decision

Done — or not done?

Now the class judges. Two worked cases first, exactly as the programme teaches them — then two cases of your own to call, out loud. The question for each is the only question that matters in this job: done, or not done? And if not done — name the missing shot.

There is no credit for saying “looks fine.” There is credit for saying exactly what is missing. That is the skill. That is the job.

Call the verdict

The two worked cases from the lesson are Cases 1 and 2 — call them before you open the answer, even so. Cases 3 and 4 are yours: judge each file, then open the verdict and check whether you named the same missing shot.

Case 1 · Grass. The after photos show a beautifully striped lawn, clean mower lines, neat edges — all close views of one patch. There is no wide photo of the full lot.

Case 2 · Secure. The front door's new lock is photographed cleanly, before and after. The order said the back window was broken. There is no photo of that window, boarded or otherwise.

Case 3 · Grass. Befores of the full lot, wide and close afters, edges clean — the file looks complete. But there is not one photo of the work happening: no mower running, no trimmer in hand, nothing between before and after.

Case 4 · Secure. Every lock is photographed before, during, and after, and every board is in the file. But the processor, checking carefully, sees the lockbox in the after photo is set to a different code than the one the order states.

Say it in class

“Do not tell me it looks good. Tell me what is missing. In this job, the missing shot is the verdict.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

Here is how the judging works. The teacher shows a photo set. For each one, the question is the same: done, or not done? If the answer is “not done,” it is only half an answer — the missing shot must be named. Not “the photos aren't great.” The missing shot, by name: the wide after photo of the whole lot. The board photo. A patch of neat grass does not prove a whole lawn was cut, and a new front lock does not prove the back of the house is shut. Learning to say exactly what is missing is the skill this whole class has been walking toward.

How to run it, step by step

  1. Work the two taught cases first, slowly, so the class sees how a verdict is built.
  2. Then judge fresh cases in pairs — one grass, one secure — verdict and missing shot said out loud.
  3. Refuse “looks fine” kindly, every time, and ask the follow-up: “What is missing?”
  4. Credit the naming, not the confidence. A quiet trainee who names the missing shot has done the job.

If you've done this work before

You already do this at a desk every day — this exercise just gives the class your eyes, one verdict at a time. The sentence to leave them with is the professional one: a verdict is a claim about proof, not about effort. The crew may truly have cut the whole lot and boarded the window. If the file cannot show it, the honest verdict is still “not proven done” — and sending it back is not an insult to the crew. It is the job protecting them, too.

The line to remember: “A verdict is a claim about proof, not about effort. Not proven done is an honest verdict — and a useful one.”

The proof — what these cases are

Cases 1 and 2 are the programme's own worked examples for this session, carried exactly: the striped lawn with no wide shot, and the new front lock with no board photo. Cases 3 and 4 are practice cases built for this page from the same rules — a missing “during” stage, and a lockbox code that does not match the order — and they are labelled as practice, here and in the logic notes. All four are descriptions of photo sets, as the session prescribes: the worked examples are described in words and stay as words.

Chapter 6 · Retrieval

One line each. What does “done” look like?

Notes shut, one more time. Before the class leaves, every trainee owes two lines, from memory, in their own words — what “done” looks like for grass, and what “done” looks like for secure. Not the teacher's lines. Theirs.

If the class can say these two lines without opening a page, the class worked.

Say it in class

“One line each. What does done look like for grass? One line each. What does done look like for secure?”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

The answer, in the programme's own shape: a full lot cut, trimmed, edged, and cleared, proven by before, during, and after photos — wide and close — with date-stamps where the order requires them. A trainee's line does not need those exact words. It needs the pieces: the whole lot, all four words of the work, all three stages of the proof, and the order deciding the stamps. A line missing a piece is a good line to repair together, out loud, kindly.

How to listen for a complete line

  1. Whole lot — not a patch, not the front only.
  2. Cut, trimmed, edged, cleared — all four.
  3. Before, during, after — wide and close.
  4. Date-stamps where the order requires them — the order, not a habit, decides.

If you've done this work before

Notice the line is a QC checklist wearing a sentence's clothes. A trainee who can say it can also check a file with it — and that is the point of ending here rather than on a summary slide. The class does not leave with notes about grass. It leaves with the instrument it will use on every grass file it ever touches.

The line to remember: “Done, for grass: the whole lot, all four words, all three stages — wide, close, and stamped where the order says so.”

The proof — where the line comes from

This retrieval and its expected shape are the session's own closing exercise, carried as written. The wording above is the teacher's reference for listening, not a script trainees must repeat word for word — the session is explicit that the answers come back in the trainees' own words, and count when the pieces are all there.

If this is all new to you

The answer, in the programme's own shape: every exterior lock changed, the lockbox code exact, every broken entry boarded, every lock and every board photographed before, during, and after — after permission, never before it. Listen for the last part especially. A secure line that lists the locks and boards but forgets the permission has missed the job's first part — the part that comes before the crew even leaves.

How to listen for a complete line

  1. Permission first — the gate answered before anyone moved.
  2. Every exterior lock changed — every one.
  3. The lockbox code exact — as the order states.
  4. Every broken entry boarded, and every lock and board photographed, before, during, and after.

If you've done this work before

The two closing lines together are the whole session in a trainee's pocket: one job judged by its proof of a surface, the other by its proof of a list — both judged only after permission, both worthless without photos. If the class leaves saying these lines the way they would check a file, Session 7 can start at speed. If they can't, this — not new material — is what the next opening recall is for.

The line to remember: “Done, for secure: permission first, every lock changed, the code exact, every entry boarded — and every bit of it photographed.”

The proof — where the line comes from

As with grass, this is the session's own closing retrieval with its expected answer, carried as written — including its final clause, “after permission, never before it,” which is the gate rule from Slide 1 arriving home at the end of the class, where the programme puts it.

Chapter 6 · The close

A house the street can trust again.

A house with a cared-for face and a shut door is a house the street can trust again. Her lawn no longer shouts. Her doors no longer invite. The first two jobs are done — and proven done, which in this work is the same sentence said twice.

But winter is coming — and an empty house in winter is in danger from the inside. That is Class 7.

Say it in class

“Grass is the house's face. Secure is the permission slip for every job after it. A house with a cared-for face and a shut door is a house the street can trust again.”

Open a point for the full notes

If this is all new to you

If you remember nothing else from tonight: grass is the face — cut, trimmed, edged, cleared, proven wide and close, and cut again on a diary so the face never slips back. And secure is the permission slip — every lock changed, the code exact, every broken entry boarded, every item photographed, and all of it only after permission. Two jobs, two lines, one house the street can trust again. Everything else is in these notes whenever you need it again.

The whole class, step by step

  1. She arrived with an order, and the order walked eleven stops.
  2. Her grass was cut — the first job — and her recut went on a diary.
  3. Her doors were secured — the permission slip — lock, code, and boards.
  4. Every step was proven, and the class learned to judge the proof: done, or not done, and the missing shot named.
  5. Winter is next. The work moves inside her walls.

If you've done this work before

Close by noticing what the class now holds that it didn't this morning: not two job descriptions, but a way of judging any job. Face or permission slip, wide or item-by-item, diary or once-and-proven — every job in the rest of this course will sort itself by the questions learned today. That is why these two jobs are taught first, and taught this slowly.

The line to remember: “Grass is the face. Secure is the permission slip. A cared-for face and a shut door — that is a house the street can trust again.”

The proof — where the close comes from

The closing lines and the cliffhanger are the session's own, carried as written: the two-line memory anchor, and winter waiting as the bridge into Session 7. Nothing on this slide adds a fact the class has not already met — a close should gather a lesson, not smuggle in a new one.

If this is all new to you

A taster, honestly labelled as one. An empty house in winter is in danger from the inside: water sitting in her pipes can freeze, and frozen water does not ask permission. She is also still holding whatever her family left behind, room by room. And somebody has to walk through her, look at everything, and write down exactly what they find. Those are next class's three jobs — winterization, debris, and inspection — and every one of them walks through the door today's secure shut, onto the ground today's grass made presentable.

How today hands over to next class

  1. The secure makes her a safe workplace — next class's crews walk in through it.
  2. The grass keeps her face — next class works on what the street cannot see.
  3. The verdict habit travels: winter work will be judged exactly the same way, shot by missing shot.

If you've done this work before

End on the stakes, plainly: the cheapest job in this industry prevents the most expensive damage, and the class is about to meet it. A house that survives winter is usually a house somebody winterized on time — one more first job, done before it was urgent, exactly like the two they learned today.

The line to remember: “Today she was made presentable and safe. Next class, she is made ready to survive the cold.”

The proof — a preview, not a lesson

This drawer names next session's three jobs and nothing more — no steps, no rules, no numbers are taught here, because they belong to Session 7 and will be taught there in full. The one claim on this slide is the session's own cliffhanger: an empty house in winter is in danger from the inside.

All slides

Class 6 — The Work I: Grass + Secure. Twelve slides: the recall, the two first jobs, their proof, the verdict, and the close. Tap any slide to jump straight to it.

The logic behind this class

For the teacher, not the class: how this page was built, what it refuses to claim, and how to run it. Everything on the slides names its home in its own notes; this page gathers the honest labels in one place.

How this class is built

  • One house, still. The same fictional 1972 house from Class 1, carrying the name the class gave her, now receives her first two jobs. She is a teaching character, not a real property, and no slide presents her as one.
  • The session, whole. This page carries Session 6 of the programme in full: the eleven-stops and gate recall, grass (four words, two kinds of cut, the diary, three-stage proof, date-stamps by the order), the four roles and the RFO guard, secure (three parts, the strictest proof, permission first), the photo-verdict decision, the two closing retrieval lines, and the winter cliffhanger. Nothing in the session was cut to fit the page.
  • No invented numbers. This session teaches work, not statistics, so the page invents none. Where a requirement is stated, it is labelled the programme's way — typical, always check the order. Where an example is a teaching pattern rather than a fact, its drawer says so.
  • Cases 3 and 4 are practice. The verdict exercise's first two cases are the programme's own worked examples. Its last two are built for this page from the same stated rules — a missing “during” stage, a lockbox code that differs from the order — and are labelled as practice in the slide's notes.

The guards kept on this page

  • The RFO line. The processor prepares the file up to ready; the owner marks Ready For Office himself. The page teaches the guard as a guard, never as a step the processor takes.
  • PPW is ours. The office engine is named as the office's own system, never a client portal — the same distinction the programme keeps everywhere.
  • Permission before movement. The gate, and HOLD-and-escalate when the answer is unclear, open the class, govern the secure, and close the retrieval. The page never shows work starting on an unclear answer.
  • No real anything. No real client, company, work order, address, price, or lockbox code appears anywhere on this page. The code slide teaches “exactly as the order states” without printing any code.
  • Photos described, not faked. The session's worked photo examples are described in words and stay as words, as the programme prescribes; the illustrations on this page are labelled as showing the work type, not any real job.

What isn't proven — the open questions, honestly

  • Every “required (typical)” list on this page is the programme's typical shape. A real order's rulebook governs a real job, and may differ in items, photo counts, and stamps. The page teaches trainees to check the order precisely because this page cannot settle it for them.
  • The four roles are the programme's division of the work, told as people. Real offices combine and rename roles; the page says so in the drawers, and teaches the parts rather than the titles.
  • The lawn's step-by-step “shouting” is a teaching illustration of how vacancy reads to a street, not a measured timeline. Its drawer labels it as such.
  • The eleven stops and the gate are recalled from Classes 4 and 5 of this programme, as Session 6 prescribes; this page leans on them rather than re-teaching them, and a class that cannot recall them needs the earlier pages, not a longer version of this one.

Running the class from this page

  • Open cold. Slide 1 is a recall before it is a welcome — notes shut, her name first, the eleven stops and the gate in under five minutes. Do not re-teach Class 5; ask the questions that lead back to it.
  • Keep the two lines visible. Grass is the face; secure is the permission slip. Return to them at every chapter change — the class is built to hang on them.
  • Protect the verdict. If time runs short, cut discussion elsewhere — never the photo verdict on Slide 10. “Done, or not done, and the missing shot by name” is what the class keeps.
  • End on their lines, not yours. Slides 11 and 12 only work if the two “done” lines come back in the trainees' own words before the teacher's reference versions are opened.
  • This page is the spine, not a guest. If a live Muse segment joins the class, it belongs in the Muse app, projected, in one short mid-class slot — and this page can still carry the whole lesson if the connection ever fails.

Where it all came from

Every drawer on the slides names its home. In short:

  • Session 6 — The Work I: Grass + Secure — of this programme's class blueprint and schedule: the story spine, the four words of a cut, initial and recut, the recut diary, the three-stage proof, the date-stamp rule, the four roles, the RFO guard, the three parts of an Initial Secure, the secure proof and handling, the two worked verdict cases, the teacher's SAY lines, the closing retrieval answers, the memory anchor, and the winter cliffhanger.
  • Classes 4 and 5 of the same programme, leaned on for the retrieval: the permission gate and its HOLD-and-escalate rule, and the eleven stops of one work order's journey.
  • Plus the earlier classes for the house herself — born 1972, named once in Class 1, emptied in Class 3, served by the system in Class 4, and ordered in Class 5.

This is the demo version of Class 6 from the preservation training programme — shared so the teacher can look it over before the full class is built. Our house is a teaching character, made up for the story; the pictures are illustrations, not a real property, and they show work types, not real jobs. Everything here is a teaching example — no real clients, work orders, prices, codes, or company details anywhere on the page.
